extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, early-career mathematicians, and faculty (academic mathematicians seeking career/research/advising guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice for mathematicians on mentoring students, choosing between industry and academia, navigating tenure, professional conduct, and doing mathematical research effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional mental-health resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution can provide some help. There are campus psychiatrists and counselors who have considerable experience dealing with the peculiar stresses and disorders that come from academic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is easy to have a session with such a person, and he/she can make a number of useful suggestions. If a student shows signs of mental-health difficulty, point them toward counselling rather than attempting to handle everything yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not handle difficult student situations in isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: The main point is that you should not try to deal with a difficult situation like this in isolation. Talk to people. Get some help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult experienced colleagues, departmental administrators, or campus services. Colleagues who have had similar trials can give tips; use department experience and avoid making unilateral decisions in complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a terminal Master's for persistently struggling/disruptive students
rubrics_metrics.description: A student who is mentally unstable and perhaps disruptive is probably not doing well in his/her studies either. It might be appropriate to get him/her a terminal Masters Degree and gently ease him/her out the door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If departmental precedent exists for handling such cases, follow it. Use this option compassionately as an exit path when remediation is ineffective or student conduct impedes progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: When applying to industry, emphasize team/people skills and demonstrable contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: People experienced with working in the private sector point out that academic recruiters are looking for 'smart' while industrial recruiters are looking for 'team players who can make a contribution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play up problem-solving skills, people skills, and concrete contributions (software, collaborations, applied projects). The interviewer is not going to fish for your best qualities — present them explicitly and make a case that your skill set meshes with the company and its goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight applied/technical fields valued by non-academic employers
rubrics_metrics.description: Fields important to a non-academic employer may include computer science, financial modeling, statistics, operations research, numerical analysis, [and] engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't necessarily need formal coursework; practical exposure (projects, software you built, taught courses, collaborations with engineers) counts. Be ready to demonstrate applied skills and relevant experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand industry vs academia tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: In industry you typically don’t have complete discretion in the problems that you work on. The point is to get results. In industry you will probably get a raise every year, and you may be up for promotion every four or five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh autonomy and intellectual freedom in academia against more frequent raises, promotions, and potentially larger financial rewards in industry. Recognize different expectations about problem selection and the goal-orientation of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for security and publication constraints in classified work
rubrics_metrics.description: If you work at a place like NSA, much of your work cannot be published in the usual venues. Anything that you want to publish in the 'outside world' has to be cleared by a superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand workplace restrictions (no bringing work home, limits on devices, restricted speech around visitors). Expect some research to be unpublishable except via internal or restricted channels; adapt to those institutional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the multi-layered tenure evaluation process
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a highly structured, multi-layered process for evaluating tenure cases. The Department, the Chair, the Dean, the Provost, the Chancellor, and the Board of Trustees all pass judgment on every tenure case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know that external letters from distinguished faculty are commonly solicited to assess stature and contributions. Your work will be judged by leaders in the field across refereeing, grants, invitations, and published contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish an independent research program by proving good theorems and publishing papers
rubrics_metrics.description: You are trying to establish yourself as a player in an area of mathematical research. You do so by proving some good theorems and publishing some papers that report on those theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: find problems that interest you, ensure they fit into the current flow of the field, choose problems you can make progress on, write papers of publication quality, submit and shepherd them through review to acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose problems that interest you and fit the field's ongoing flow
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to find problems that are of interest to you, will give you the fire in the guts, ... The problems of the first stripe must also be problems that fit naturally into the current ongoing flow of mathematics as it is practiced today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid problems that bring only personal satisfaction but little professional recognition (example: obsessing over obscure puzzles like 'EMIRP numbers'). Aim for problems where leaders in the field will see the value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select problems you have a chance of solving
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to find problems that you have a chance of solving, or at least of making a significant contribution towards their understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaining the judgment to weigh solvability takes experience: attend seminars, conferences, talk to people, consult problem lists and online resources to calibrate problem difficulty and your fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce publishable manuscripts and handle the editorial/referee process
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to actually get the papers written—and written in a form and style that is of publication quality. You need to get the papers submitted to journals, get them through the editorial process, and get them accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many talented mathematicians stumble on writing, polishing, submitting, or responding to referees. Maintain discipline, tenacity, and the maturity to make requested edits and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate contiguous uninterrupted blocks of deep work time
rubrics_metrics.description: It is nearly impossible to do serious mathematical research for more than four or five hours in a day. Go some place where you absolutely, positively cannot be interrupted and sit in front of a tablet of paper and think hard and calculate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for several hours (e.g., four productive hours) of focused work multiple days per week. Research is not productive in frequent short snatches; allow time to organize ideas before calculation and proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt research methods to your field and personal style
rubrics_metrics.description: The shape and nature of mathematical research is ever-changing. Some people do much of their research on the computer. Some people do their research in teams. Some build physical models. Some read everything; others read little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what works for you: computational experiments, collaborations, numerical models, reading the literature, attending seminars, online resources, and team interactions are all legitimate research modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use seminars, conferences, and online resources to learn and network
rubrics_metrics.description: You must go to seminars, go to conferences, and talk to people. One of the great things about modern mathematics is that there is so much free and open communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take advantage of talks, problem lists, wikis, webpages, and chat rooms to get up to speed, find problems, and make contacts—these resources help you judge problems and connect with the community that will evaluate your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain strict professional boundaries with students to avoid harassment risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, it is a good idea to keep your personal life separate from your professional life. Never, ever do anything with a student in one of your classes except teach him/her mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include: never meet students in your office with the door closed; do not have sofas or furniture for reclining in your office; do not sit close to students; do not ever touch students; avoid extracurricular one-on-one activities (dates, bars, concerts); avoid suggestive remarks or prolonged looks. These precautions reduce vulnerability to accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle two-body hiring problems delicately and honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you, as Chair, are asked to handle a two-body situation, then my advice is to proceed with some delicacy. Show the candidates the utmost consideration, and be solicitous of their needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be candid about institutional constraints (there are no truly 'free' positions). Use networking, administrative resources for spouses, and, where possible, coordinate offers but avoid compromising departmental standards without careful consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present demonstrable outputs when seeking industrial positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever you are interviewing for a job, you should be prepared to play up your strong points and acquaint the interviewer with who you are and what you have to offer. The interviewer is not going to fish for your best qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show concrete accomplishments (software you created, courses taught, collaborations) that demonstrate fit with the company's problems. Make explicit how your academic background meshes with practical working environments.
